title: The Coward of Asaya
subtitle: The Legend of Kagemori Jūrō
teaser: He was the finest sword in the east, and too proud to lose a single bout. The registers remember him as the only man of House Asaya who ran.

sections.heading: I. The First Sword of the East
paragraphs: Before every duel, Kagemori Jūrō told the other man his name.

He said it slowly, so it would be remembered. “Kagemori Jūrō, sword master of House Asaya.” Then he stood with his hand resting on the hilt and waited for the other man to move. Nobody ever saw what happened next. There was a sound like silk tearing, and the duel was over, and the sword was back in its scabbard.
By thirty he had fought sixty-one duels and never needed to draw twice.

House Asaya was a small house. It held one castle on a bend of the river Saegi, a few hundred fields, and the only bridge for forty miles. The great lords of the east had more men and more gold. Asaya had Jūrō, and in every teahouse from the mountains to the sea, that seemed like enough.
Lord Asaya Nobuhide knew what his sword master was worth. After the fiftieth duel he gave Jūrō a scabbard of black lacquer with Jūrō’s name inlaid down its length in gold.
“A small house needs a big name,” the lord said. “You are ours.”

Jūrō wore that scabbard everywhere. Some evenings he went down to the archive and asked the old clerk to open the house register, the great book in red boards where every retainer’s name stood beside his oath. Jūrō’s was first, in the lord’s own hand. He never touched it. He only looked.
“Pride is a fine thing in a sword,” the clerk told him once, closing the book. “In a man, it has to be fed.”
Jūrō laughed. He had never gone hungry in his life.

sections.heading: II. The Bout
paragraphs: In his thirty-first spring, the shogun came to Asaya with three thousand men and a treaty.

The whole east was his but for a few small houses, and he wanted the bridge over the Saegi without the expense of a war. Asaya would keep its castle and fields and open the bridge to his armies, and both seals would go on the treaty in the great hall. Then, by custom, the swordsmen of the two houses would give a bout for the guests. Live blades, to first touch.
The shogun’s swordsman was his own son, Takemasa. He was twenty and very fast, and he had asked for the honour himself.
The night before, Lord Asaya called Jūrō to his rooms and sent the servants out.
“Tomorrow you will lose,” he said.
Jūrō thought he had misheard. “I have never lost.”
“That is why it will be worth something. Let the boy touch your sleeve. Bow. Praise his hand. A shogun whose son has beaten Kagemori Jūrō goes home happy, and a happy shogun keeps his word.”
“And Kagemori Jūrō?”
“Is alive, and so is this house. It is one bout. Nobody will think less of you.”
“I will,” said Jūrō.
The lord looked at him for a long time. “Then think less of yourself,” he said. “That is an order.”
The next morning the treaty was sealed, and the two swordsmen knelt facing each other across the mats. Jūrō meant to obey. He had already chosen the place on his sleeve.
Then Takemasa smiled and said, loud enough for the whole hall, “They say your name is known from here to the sea. After today, they will say mine.”
Jūrō did not decide anything. His hand decided. There was a sound like silk tearing, and Takemasa’s topknot fell onto the mat between them, and the hall went silent.
The shogun laughed first. He picked up his son’s hair himself and handed it back to him. “Keep this one close, Asaya,” he said. “A sword like that is worth a war.”

Within the year his clerks found a quarrel over bridge tolls, the treaty was torn, and the shogun came back with thirty thousand men. Everyone in the castle knew why. Nobody said it to Jūrō’s face. That was worse.

sections.heading: III. The Water Gate
paragraphs: The siege lasted fifty days. On the fiftieth night the rice was gone, the wells were foul, and the shogun’s lanterns lay around the castle like a second river.

Lord Asaya called his retainers into the great hall. At dawn, he said, the gates would open and he would ride out, and any man who wished could ride beside him. Every man wished it. One by one they knelt and swore to follow their lord into death, and the old clerk wrote each name into the red register beside the oath.
Jūrō went forward to kneel first. The lord stopped him with one hand.
“Not you.”

When the hall was empty, the lord put a lacquered box into his arms. Inside, wrapped in oilcloth, lay the torn treaty under the shogun’s seal and the house war record of every promise the shogun had broken.

“Out through the water gate, tonight,” the lord said. “Take it to the capital and lay it before the Emperor’s court. A shogun who breaks a sealed treaty can be stripped of his title. The court needs proof. This is the proof.”
“Send someone else,” said Jūrō. “Let me die beside you. It is the only thing I have left that is worth anything.”

“You are the only man who can get through,” said the lord. Then, more quietly: “And you have not earned a death beside me. You fed your pride, and it ate my house. Every man here will die with honour in the morning. You don’t get honour. You get the river.”
Jūrō bowed until his forehead touched the boards. He did not trust himself to speak.

He went out through the water gate at the dead of night, the box bound to his back and the golden scabbard tied across it. The river was black and very cold. He swam under the shogun’s boats with their lanterns wobbling over his head. On the far bank a sentry turned at the sound of dripping water. Jūrō drew once, and the sentry sat down in the reeds and stayed there.
From the hill above the river, he looked back.

At dawn the conch shells blew, the gates of Asaya opened, and he watched the last charge go out into thirty thousand men. By noon the castle was burning. He could see the roof of the great hall, its old cedar beams pouring out black smoke shot through with red. He watched until it fell in. Then he turned his back and walked to the capital.

sections.heading: IV. The Register
paragraphs: It took him a month to reach the capital and four more to be seen. He slept under bridges and carried loads in the river markets to eat. He kept the sword.

At last a minister of the court named Tsukimura received him in a room that smelled of plum blossom. Tsukimura had very soft hands. He did not open the box. He thanked Jūrō for his loyalty and told him to come back in three days.
On the third day Jūrō was shown into a courtyard where a brazier was burning. Tsukimura was feeding the war record of Asaya into it, one page at a time, without reading them.
“The shogun has sent the court a great deal of rice this year,” he said pleasantly. “The court is very fond of rice.”
The treaty went in last. Jūrō watched the shogun’s seal blister and run.
“You should be grateful,” the minister said. “He asked for your head as well. We told him there was no need.” He held out a scroll. “His chroniclers have already written you.”

It was the shogun’s register of the fall of Asaya, copied out for every great house in the east. It was generous to the dead. It named every retainer who had ridden out at dawn and called them loyal unto death. Honouring brave enemies cost the shogun nothing.
At the bottom, set apart, there was one more name.
Kagemori Jūrō, sword master, the only man of Asaya who broke his oath. While his lord died, he fled by the water gate in the night. Let him be known as the coward of Asaya.
The line was in a young man’s hand, and signed. Takemasa had asked for the honour himself.

Jūrō could have told the truth. But every man who had heard the order was dead, the proof was ash in a brazier, and he would have had to beg to be believed. Kagemori Jūrō did not beg. He bowed to the minister and walked out.

He walked back to the Saegi. Asaya was a black stump on the bend of the river. He waded out below the ruined water gate, sat on a stone in the current, and scraped his name off the scabbard with a pebble, one character at a time, until the gold was in the water and the lacquer was plain black.
“Take it,” he told the river. “Nobody else will.”

Then he drew the sword, and smoke poured off the blade. It was thick and black and full of red embers, and it smelled of cedar. He sheathed it and drew again. It was still there. It has never stopped.

sections.heading: V. The Nameless Blade
paragraphs: In the duelling rings, the fighters’ names are chalked on a board beside the gate. Next to his there is a blank square. The crowds call him the Nameless Blade, because they have to call him something.

He wears a straw hat low over his eyes, so that no one from the east will know his face. It is not fear. A coward should not be looked at. His hakama is dark and plain, and on the breast of his coat there is a ring of tiny holes where the crest of Asaya was unpicked.

The men who face him are young, and they come for glory. They shout their names and their fathers’ names and the names of their schools, and he waits under the hat while the smoke rolls off his blade. He has all the patience in the world. If they rush him, he draws once, and there is a sound like silk tearing. If they hang back, he comes through his own smoke in a single long thrust, and they do not see the point until it is in them.

He has explained himself only once, to a ring-master who would not open the gate without a reason. “A man who cuts open his own belly goes into the registers twice,” he said. “A man beaten in a fair duel goes into nothing. I am waiting for someone good enough.”
Nobody has been. More than once he has stood in a ring meaning to let a boy’s blade through, and every time, his hand decides. He knows now that it was never his hand. It was him.
Ask him about the smoke, and he says the castle is still burning. Ask him when it will stop, and he says nothing at all.
The registers have outlasted Asaya. In every great house in the east, boys are still taught about the coward who ran by the water gate. Nobody remembers that he had a name.
Before every duel now, the other man tells him his. Jūrō listens, and lets him finish. Then he says the only thing he ever says.
“Your name won’t be remembered. Neither will mine.”
Then the smoke comes off the blade, and the castle burns a little longer.

quote: Your name won’t be remembered. Neither will mine.
